prize_parts.citation: for the invention and realisation of optical lattice clocks, in which magic-wavelength trapping of many atoms opened the 10^-18 regime of frequency measurement and laboratory tests of gravitational redshift and fundamental physics

statement.case_for: I have changed my preferred configuration from topological insulators (B015) to optical lattice clocks (B002) with Katori and Ye as the sole part. This is a judgement on my own round-1 criteria, not a response to the count of supporters. I asked for a verified physical result, independent confirmation and quantitative agreement between laboratories. Lattice clocks meet all three: the magic-wavelength lattice removes the light shift, and Sr, Yb and Hg clocks in several independent laboratories now agree at the 10^-18 level, with the redshift resolved across millimetres. The result is a measured effect that can be checked, not an interpretation. The credit is the decisive difference from my first choice. In round 1 I argued that the topological-insulator attribution could be argued but not dissolved, and a second reading of the chair's summary and the other statements has not given me a trio that is fair to Bernevig, Hughes, Zhang (deceased), Fu, Moore and Hasan. B015 stays my first alternative because I still regard the science as confirmed and arguably overdue, and I would revisit it if the committee found a defensible credit. The clock prize is also close to my field in method: the many-body systematics and the reading of shifts in the lattice are controlled spectroscopy, which I know well enough to judge as sound.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation remains discovery versus technique. A clock is an instrument, and the 2005 prize (Hall, Hansch, with Ye sharing in it) and the 2012 prize (Wineland, Haroche) already honour the comb and ion control. My answer to the chair's question is one sentence for the citation: the new content is the magic-wavelength trapping of very many neutral atoms, which turned clock interrogation into a many-body regime where systematics are controlled below 10^-18 and where redshift, constants and dark-matter couplings become measurable in the laboratory; the comb supplied the ruler and the ion work supplied single-system control, and neither supplied that. I do not regard this as a surprise of nature in the way a new phase of matter is, so I hold the position with less enthusiasm than I held B015, and I would accept that a committee member could reasonably weigh it differently. The citation must not depend on the pending redefinition of the second. Priority between Katori, Lemonde and others on the magic-wavelength idea is unchecked by me, and the credit between Katori's first demonstration and Ye's accuracy records needs the atomic-physics members to state it.

responses.point: Eva keeps B002 first and argues that the content is distinct from the 2005 and 2012 prizes (lattice interrogation, magic wavelength, many-atom systematics, redshift tests), while accepting that the citation must make the argument explicitly and that the redefinition of the second has not happened.
responses.response: Your distinction is the one that moved me, and I have used it in my own case above. I would ask you and Stefan to report on the early-2000s chronology, since you can read the original papers and I cannot judge it. If Pottier and Lemonde or others proposed the magic wavelength in parallel, the citation should be worded around the realisation of the lattice clock and the many-atom regime and not around a claim of sole invention, which would still leave Katori and Ye as the credited pair. I also agree that the thorium and ion clocks should not be written into the citation, since they are still developing.

responses.point: Eva asks whether the prize should go to the original experiment (Katori) rather than the later, more accurate realisation (Ye), wants the priority record reviewed, and notes that Lemonde, Takamoto and the ion-clock community are not credited.
responses.response: I share your criterion, and I think it is met here only if the citation is read with care. Katori proposed the lattice and made the first strontium demonstration, and Ye's group took the accuracy, stability and many-body control to the regime that opened the physics applications. I read these as two distinct steps in one achievement and not as an original and a copy, and the record should be checked before the final ballot, as you ask. I would not delay the prize for it unless the check showed that a third person made the first demonstration. In that case I would want the committee to say so openly, even if the three-person cap then forced a hard choice.

responses.point: Bernhard prefers KPZ universality (B056) as a compact, mature and conceptually central statistical-physics result, and himself concedes that Parisi and the exact-solution authors are outside the credited names and that only his opening ballot placed it.
responses.response: I respect the conceptual weight of KPZ and I have changed in part toward your view that a clock must show what is new. Where we still differ is attribution and independence: with Parisi and the exact solutions outside the credited set, and the experimental confirmation resting mostly on one liquid-crystal system, I cannot say the credit is more secure than for the clocks. Lindroth and Kroll asked for reproduction beyond that system, and I would like you to say whether you know of any. I also withdraw my round-1 statement that the 2016 overlap for topological insulators is a small matter, because I now think you and Danielsson are right that the community would see a lineage.

responses.point: Stefan keeps B002 first, regards the credit as the cleanest on the shortlist, and acknowledges that he ranks from memory on the uncertainty figures and the origin of the magic-wavelength idea, and that the Sr and Yb community is not credited.
responses.response: I agree that the credit is the cleanest on the shortlist, and your point that clocks change what can be measured is the argument I find strongest against my own concern about technique. I would ask you to check the quoted uncertainty figures and who first articulated the idea against the record, since the citation will quote the 10^-18 figure and it should be exact. If the check reveals that the claim is weaker for one laboratory, I would qualify the wording and not drop the part. On the omitted community, I think a two-person prize is workable if the citation names the lattice clock and the regime it opened and does not claim the whole of strontium and ytterbium metrology.

uncertainties: Chronology and priority of the magic-wavelength proposal and of the first lattice-clock demonstrations (Katori, Lemonde, Pottier, others), which I cannot verify from my own expertise.

Whether the committee accepts that the lattice regime recognises something distinct from the 2005 comb and the 2012 ion-control prizes, and whether a precision capability is the right emphasis this year compared with a new state of matter.
Whether a fair, defensible credit for topological insulators (B015) exists given Bernevig, Hughes, Zhang (deceased) and the 3D contributors; if so, I would rank it closer to B002.
Whether the second should be redefined or a competing nuclear clock result appears before the announcement, which would change the framing but not, in my view, the credit.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from my profile. I have no collaboration or institutional tie to Katori, Ye, Kane, Mele or Molenkamp, or to the credited names of the alternatives. My electronic-structure and spin-dynamics work is field-adjacent to topological materials and spectroscopy at light sources, which is expertise and not a conflict. I note the disclosures by Olsson, Kroll and Lindroth for B002 and do not regard them as disqualifying.
